summary: Describes HTTP Datagrams, a way to send multiplexed, potentially unreliable datagrams inside an HTTP connection. In HTTP/3 they can use the QUIC DATAGRAM extension, and where that is unavailable or undesirable, the Capsule Protocol conveys them. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Web connections normally deliver everything in order. This adds a way to send small, quick messages that may get lost, a bit like tossing notes through the same window.

questions: how do http datagrams work over http/2
subtitle: A way to send small, possibly unreliable datagrams inside an HTTP connection, plus a capsule format for when the transport cannot.

tldr.problem: Some HTTP extensions, such as an unreliable version of CONNECT, need unreliable delivery, but HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 over TCP only offer reliable streams and HTTP/3 may not always use QUIC DATAGRAM frames.
tldr.mechanism: HTTP Datagrams are tied to an HTTP request. In HTTP/3 they ride in QUIC DATAGRAM frames, negotiated with the SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM setting. Otherwise the Capsule Protocol carries them as DATAGRAM capsules, a type-length-value stream on the request's data stream.
tldr.outcome: Extensions that define new HTTP upgrade tokens can use datagrams across all HTTP versions, and intermediaries can forward unknown capsule types untouched.

today: RFC 9297 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2022. Its metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Why HTTP Needs Datagrams
sections.content:
HTTP extensions sometimes need transport features such as the unreliable delivery offered by the QUIC DATAGRAM extension. The RFC gives examples: an unreliable version of the CONNECT method and unreliable delivery for WebSockets.

HTTP Datagrams are a convention for conveying bidirectional and potentially unreliable datagrams inside an HTTP connection, with multiplexing when possible. They are associated with HTTP requests but are not part of message content, and they are compatible with all versions of HTTP. The Capsule Protocol conveys them using reliable delivery where the QUIC DATAGRAM frame is unavailable or undesirable, or the transport is only reliable, such as HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 over TCP.
sections.eli5: Some web tricks need fast little messages that are fine to lose. This RFC says how to send them over the web connection you already have.

sections.title: HTTP Datagrams Across HTTP Versions
sections.content:
Every HTTP Datagram is associated with an HTTP request. What is available depends on the HTTP version.

  • HTTP/3: the QUIC DATAGRAM frame can provide demultiplexing and unreliable delivery.
  • HTTP/2: the framing layer provides demultiplexing, but unreliable delivery is unavailable, so the Capsule Protocol is used.
  • HTTP/1.x: requests are strictly serialized, so neither demultiplexing nor unreliable delivery is available, and the Capsule Protocol is used.

Datagrams MUST only be sent with a request that explicitly supports them. Existing methods such as GET and POST define no such semantics. A receiver that gets a datagram for a request with no known semantics MUST terminate the request, and in HTTP/3 the stream is aborted with H3_DATAGRAM_ERROR (0x33). Extensions MAY override this by defining their own negotiation and semantics.
sections.eli5: Some web connections can toss notes and some cannot. Where tossing is impossible, the notes get tucked into the ordinary line instead.

sections.title: HTTP/3 Datagrams and the Setting
sections.content:
In HTTP/3 the Datagram Data field of a QUIC DATAGRAM frame holds a Quarter Stream ID followed by the HTTP Datagram Payload (which may be empty). The Quarter Stream ID is a variable-length integer: the value of the client-initiated bidirectional stream divided by four, because HTTP requests use streams whose IDs are divisible by four. The largest legal QUIC stream ID is 2^62-1, so the largest legal Quarter Stream ID is 2^60-1, and a larger value is an HTTP/3 connection error of type H3_DATAGRAM_ERROR.

A datagram too short to parse is also that error. Datagrams received after the stream's receive side is closed are silently dropped. If the stream does not exist yet, the receiver either drops the datagram silently or buffers it briefly, on the order of a round trip. Prioritization is left to future extensions.

An endpoint says it will receive HTTP/3 Datagrams by sending SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM (0x33) with a value of 1. The value MUST be 0 or 1, otherwise the receiver MUST terminate the connection with H3_SETTINGS_ERROR. QUIC DATAGRAM frames MUST NOT be sent until the setting has been both sent and received with value 1. With 0-RTT, a client MAY remember the server's value, and a server that accepts 0-RTT MUST send a value greater than or equal to the earlier one.
sections.eli5: Each little note is labeled with which web request it belongs to. Before tossing notes, both sides must say 'yes, I can catch them'.

sections.title: Capsules and the Capsule Protocol
sections.content:
The Capsule Protocol is a sequence of type-length-value tuples that definitions of new HTTP upgrade tokens can choose to use. A capsule has a Capsule Type, a Capsule Length (in bytes, and it can be zero) and a Capsule Value, with the first two being variable-length integers. It lets endpoints reliably communicate request-related information end-to-end, even through HTTP intermediaries.

The capsules travel on the request's data stream: the bytes after the header section of the request and the final successful (2xx) or upgraded (101) response. In HTTP/1.x only the last request on a connection can start the Capsule Protocol. In HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 it is the bytes in DATA frames of that stream, and the protocol can only be used with the CONNECT method.

Endpoints MUST silently drop capsules of unknown type and skip to the next one. Intermediaries SHOULD forward unknown capsules unchanged. The protocol MUST NOT be used with messages containing Content-Length, Content-Type or Transfer-Encoding, and status codes 204, 205 and 206 MUST NOT be sent on responses that use it. Receivers SHOULD avoid buffering a whole Capsule Value before handling it, since that can consume flow control and deadlock.
sections.eli5: A capsule is a labeled box: a tag for what it is, how big it is, then the contents. If you see a box type you do not know, you skip it and open the next one.

sections.title: Errors and the Capsule-Protocol Header
sections.content:
A receiver that hits an error in the Capsule Protocol MUST treat it as a malformed or incomplete HTTP message. A capsule payload must contain exactly the fields described: extra or missing bytes are errors, and redundant length encodings MUST be checked for consistency. A truncated last capsule on a cleanly closed stream is also an error.

The Capsule-Protocol header field is a Structured Field Item whose value MUST be a Boolean; any other type is handled as if the field were absent. A true value says the Capsule Protocol is in use, and false means the same as absent. Receivers MUST ignore unknown parameters. Intermediaries MAY use it to process datagrams for unknown upgrade tokens. It MUST NOT appear on responses with a status other than 101 and outside 2xx. Endpoints SHOULD send it to simplify intermediary processing.
sections.eli5: If a box is the wrong size or cut off, treat the whole message as broken. A sticker on the outside, Capsule-Protocol, tells helpers along the way that boxes are inside.

sections.title: The DATAGRAM Capsule and Intermediaries
sections.content:
The DATAGRAM capsule has type 0x00 and a payload that is the HTTP Datagram Payload (which can be empty). Datagrams sent this way have the same semantics, and the same sending and processing restrictions, as those in QUIC DATAGRAM frames.

An intermediary MAY re-encode datagrams between the two forms, but not unless it has identified the Capsule Protocol on that request stream. Capsules on a stream are delivered reliably and in order, but re-encoding into QUIC DATAGRAM frames could cause loss or reordering.

If an intermediary receives a datagram in a QUIC DATAGRAM frame and forwards on a connection that supports such frames, it SHOULD NOT convert it to a capsule. If it is too large for the frame, the intermediary SHOULD drop it. Converting would let datagrams grow arbitrarily large without loss, which misrepresents path properties and defeats methods such as DPLPMTUD. A capsule can in theory carry a payload of length 2^62-1, so implementations SHOULD discard a known-unusable length without buffering.

New extensions that use HTTP Datagrams SHOULD use the Capsule Protocol, to ease support for versions other than HTTP/3 and interoperability with intermediaries.
sections.eli5: A helper in the middle should not wrap a quick note into the slow reliable line, because that hides how big a note the road can really carry.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
Sending HTTP Datagrams in QUIC DATAGRAM frames requires SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM, so it "sticks out": probing clients can learn whether a server supports them. Servers may want to hide that, so it is best for all implementations that support the feature to always send the setting. Because the Capsule Protocol is limited to new upgrade tokens, it is not directly reachable from Web Platform APIs such as JavaScript in browsers. Definitions of new upgrade tokens that use it need their own security analysis.

IANA registered the HTTP/3 setting SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM (0x33, default 0), the HTTP/3 error code H3_DATAGRAM_ERROR (0x33, a datagram or Capsule Protocol parse error), and the field name Capsule-Protocol. It also created the HTTP Capsule Types registry for a 62-bit space, initially holding DATAGRAM (0x00). Types of the form 0x29 * N + 0x17 are reserved to exercise the rule that unknown types are ignored.
sections.eli5: Offering to catch notes can reveal that your server does fancy things, so everyone should offer anyway. The official lists now have the new names and numbers.
